Review of manuscript: Streaks on Martian Slopes are Dry
By V. T. Bickel & A. Valantinas
General Overview
Slope streaks (SS) are narrow, elongated, fan-shaped features which range from about a few meters
to several kilometers in length with a width in the range of tens of meters to 1m following the
downslope topography of the terrain. They display in most cases an increasing width along the
downslope direction. They appear as darker (DSS) and brighter (BSS) varieties. Slope streaks can
appear anytime in the Mars year in the equatorial and subequatorial regions of Mars. Slope streaks
are generally thought to form in single events, appearing to be formed within a short temporal span.
They gradually fade over decades.
SS are of special interest because they represent one of the most widespread and largest active
geological processes on the surface of present-day Mars. The origin of slope streaks and their
formation mechanism is to-date not yet understood and highly debated.
A "wet" mechanism suggests that a fluid, e.g. liquid water, could be responsible for their creation,
possibly as a result of groundwater springs, melting surface ice, or the formation of brines. In the
opposing view, a "dry" mechanism suggests that “dust avalanches” are responsible. These, in turn,
could be caused by air fall deposits, subsurface melting, or localized disturbances – ranging from
rockfalls, meteorite impacts to tectonic activity. Both of these explanations have limitations when
it comes to explaining observed slope streaks.
In view of the ongoing debate on the origin of DSS and BSS any research which can shed additional
light on slope streaks is of interest.
Recurring slope lineae (RSL) are narrow, downslope-trending features, darker than their surroundings,
that gradually extend primarily in warm seasons, fade and recur annually (Dundas et al., 2017).
Distinguishing SS from RSL, dunes, and shadowed topographical features, to name only a few
geomorphic features which can look very similar, can be an extremely difficult task, especially when
only images are available which were taken under very different observational conditions.
The authors (Bickel and Valantinas) use grayscale images for their investigation generated by the
Context Camera (CTX) with a resolution of up to ca. 6 m/px onboard NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance
Orbiter (operating from Nov. 2006 until today), and state in their paper that they could use a deep
learning-driven detector which is able to localize about 20 % of all BSS and 55 % of all DSS in a given
CTX image. Based on this, they conclude that the actual number of bright and dark streaks observable
at the CTX-scale on the surface of Mars are ~65,000 and ~970,000. Finding that their detection boxes
contain an average of 2.33 streaks due to overlap and collocation they claim that the total number of
BSS and DSS on Mars at the CTX resolution should amount to 150’000 and 2’260’000 BSS and DSS,
respectively. Using their global gestatistical findings, they furthermore claim that their research
- shows that slope streaks modify less than 0.1 % of the Martian surface, but transport several global
storm equivalents of dust per Mars year, potentially playing a major role in the surface-to-
atmosphere dust exchange.

Production of training set for the investigation
As SSs gradually fade from dark to bright, a clear definition needs to be given in what in the
classification algorithm considers to be a DSS or BSS. The authors use 40 CTX images given in Table S2
for training and testing in what they call a globally-distributed data set. The reviewer’s analysis of
these 40 images, their distribution on a surface map of Mars and the recognized SS in those images
reveal a variety of problems. The reviewer assumes that the fact that many of the 40 images overlap
originates from the wish to include newly-created SS with older SS in the training set, thus to
somehow acquire examples from dark and bright SS in the training data set (In the supplement the
authors show the newly-created SS taken from some of the images). After studying the image
collection used, the reviewer does not agree with the authors that they were able to produce a
globally-distributed data set.
Our reply: As the reviewer mentions, slope streaks slowly and continuously fade, where their
appearance is dominated by their physical state, but also by the imaging geometry and
illumination, as thoroughly discussed by e.g. Valantinas et al. (2021,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pss.2021.105373). Thus, there is no clear boundary between dark and
bright slope streaks. We added a sentence to the Results section to clarify our understanding of
dark and bright streaks:
Here, ‘dark’ streaks include recently-formed streaks that appear dark in CTX images, and ‘bright’
streaks refer to old, partially-faded streaks that appear bright in CTX images (Fig. 1A,1B).
Our training and testing dataset is constructed using CTX images taken across the three main slope
streak hotspots: Amazonis, Tharsis, and Arabia, as identified by numerous previous, manual (and
unbiased) surveys. Importantly, no earlier study has found any indications that slope streak
morphology would vary geographically. Other criteria we considered when constructing our
training and testing datasets are 1) a range of observation and illumination geometries that reflect
the properties of the CTX images used by the global mosaic and 2) a range of image quality states,
such as haze and oversaturation. We point out that the geographic distribution of CTX images used
by earlier work that looked into the automated detection of slope streaks such as Wang et al.
(2017) is nearly identical to our selection. For those reasons we are convinced that our training and
testing datasets are indeed globally-distributed – and more importantly – globally representative.

Concerning Few-Shot Learning
AI techniques have problems to rapidly generalize from a few examples. In addition, AI methods rely
on learning from large-scale data. The question of how to find models of categories from very few
instances has been discussed for more than twenty years and has recently found renewed interest in
the literature due to the success of large-language models. Few-Shot Learning is of course of
particular interest in cases where we have very few images which can be used as training examples.
When it comes to SS the question must be asked whether Few-Shot Learning really brings an
advantage in view of the fact that with the collection of high-quality Mars images available we have
hundreds of thousands of very easy recognizable SS at hand. It may be that Few-Shot Learning really
is able to find new categories of SS not observed before, but it may also be possible that a Few-Shot
Learning approach may severely underperform a conventional approach to building an image
collection for training the CNN. Keeping in mind that the authors want to draw some far-reaching
conclusions from their research, the reviewer is surprised to see that they just assume that Few-Shot
Learning is the way to go. If they want to use Few-Shot Learning they need to bring forward the
evidence that it is useful in this particular case (the reviewer has looked at the cited papers of the
authors).
As the authors to not communicate their reasoning for choosing their approach, and given the
relevance of the training set for their investigation they need to outline a sampling plan for the
inclusion of images and, in particular, need to provide a clear-cut definition of what dark and bright
means. They also should make the training data set (the 1007 and 147 DDS and BSS) available to the
community.
Our reply: Pre-trained object detectors are able to achieve remarkable performance even when
trained with extremely few labels, see e.g. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2203.04291 - in
addition, CTX might have imaged hundreds of thousands of slope streaks (as our work proves for
the first time), but manually labeling a substantial number of those slope streaks in images is
extremely time-consuming. We invested a significant amount of time to create a very large training
and testing dataset with 1200 individual features extracted from 40 CTX images, which is notably
larger than the dataset created and used by e.g. Wang et al. (2017, 888 labels in 28 images).
Our usage of the term “few-shot learning” is meant to communicate the fact that we employ a
deep learning method, but without having access to the very large label datasets usually used for
deep learning models (with hundreds of thousands of labels). The studies referenced in the
manuscript have proven numerous times that a few-shot learning approach – with as few labels for
16
training of a detector as 61 labels (Bickel et al., 2024b, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-024-03685-
3) – can be used to successfully map geomorphic and atmospheric features across various planets,
as referenced in the manuscript. We added a new sentence to the Online Methods section that
specifies our usage of the term “few-shot learning”:
Here, the usage of the term ‘few-shot learning’ accounts for the fact that the number of slope streak
labels available for training and testing is lower than in traditional deep learning which commonly uses
tens of thousands of labels. Importantly, past studies have demonstrated that a few-shot learning
approach can successfully map geomorphic and atmospheric features across various planetary bodies
and datasets (Bickel et al., 2020b; 2022; 2023; 2024a,b; Conway, Bickel et al., 2024; Ruesch & Bickel,
2023; Mills et al., 2024).
We will make our training and testing datasets available to the public after acceptance of the
manuscript, on the University of Bern’s BORIS archive (in addition to the slope streak dataset).
Separability of individual SSs
As the author show in Fig. 9, SSs can manifest themselves as isolated features on a slope or in groups,
where individual SSs can be very close. This is visible when one compares patch 3 with patch 6 in Fig.
9. It makes obviously a difference for the statistical consideration whether many SSs which are close
to each other are counted as individual streaks, or a whole group is detected as a single SS.
Computing the mean number of streaks in the boxes may be an oversimplified way to estimate the
real number of streaks, as in many cases SS are not fully contained in the bounding boxes. The
reviewer has not found any discussion on the separability of individual SSs and what is required for
their separability. How this can affect the different research questions they want to analyze in the
paper is not adequately discussed.

under- or over-estimate the actual number of slope streaks in a given region.

the detector should be correct. However, past experience with object detectors being applied to
extremely large and heterogeneous orbital image datasets has shown that the testset performance is

Our reply: The cited statement in the manuscript reflects a well-documented phenomenon of
applications of deep learning to extremely large planetary remote sensing datasets. Past surveys
using deep learning to map features in extremely large image datasets on the Moon, Mars,
Mercury, and other bodies have repeatedly shown that the testset performance is usually better
than the ‘real world’ performance, i.e., the performance of the detector in the full image datasets,
which might feature hundreds of thousands of images or more. The reason for the observed drop
of performance is the fact that no training and testing dataset with ~hundreds to ~thousands of
labels is possibly able to fully reflect all the geomorphic features, terrains, image artefacts, and
various oddities (cosmic ray, bit flips, transmission errors, sensor noise, etc.) contained in a real,
global, multi-decade image dataset. We include the cited statement in the manuscript to make a
reader aware of that important fact.
We note that once a first global scan is completed, as represented by this work, that earlier
knowledge gap concerning many of the above mentioned artefacts and oddities is closed, which in
turn will uniquely enable future, better, and more accurate mapping efforts.
The authors write “We do not find any direct or indirect evidence for any negative effect of the
scanned CTX images on the mapping outputs, such as potentially caused by cloud cover, shadowing,
haze, and data artifacts. We point out that Dickson et al. (2023) carefully selected the images that
make up the global mosaic to minimize any such negative impacts”. Cloud cover, dust storms, etc. are
all seasonal effects. As the authors have looked in their investigation for these effects and could not
find any, the reader is interested that they share their findings with her/him and the reader would
also probably like to learn how they could conclude this.
Furthermore, the authors write: “The extremely wide range of slope streak morphologies identified by
the detector (Fig. S1) provides evidence for a robust and capable detector”. The reviewer needs to
remind the authors that you can have a detector capable of seeing a diverse variety of features
(classes) but which can completely underestimate/overestimate specific categories of morphologies.

comment above). We did not identify any such negative impacts, despite significant efforts, as
reported in the manuscript.

Many of the variables they use (e.g., Equivalent Hydrogen (WEH), wind speed, etc.) to correlate their
SS occurances are quantities which are not only difficult to measure, but rely on many assumptions.
In addition these quantities are known at completely different resolution compared to the mapping of
SSs with the help of the CTX images. For example, WEH determination is in itself an extremely difficult
process which in essence requires the estimation of the soil’s water content from measurements of
neutrons. In order to map the water abundance in a given subsurface layer from orbital neutron
measurements one has to develop a procedure which restores the water abundance at different
points of the soil’s volume on the basis of the measured neutrons (of different energies at different
orbital points). Besides a good model for the detector a model for the atmosphere and a model for
the Martian subsurface is needed. These maps which the authors are using were produced as global
maps! They have to be used with uttermost care when you look into specific regions.
Correlating the SS observations found with wind speeds one should also not forget that the seasonal
wind intensities are obtained using what is called a “climatology average solar” scenario. Due to the
coarse resolution of the General Circulation Model (GCM), small-scale variations in topography
remain unconsidered in the simulation runs. Values are often estimated for daytime-maximum
22
surface temperatures for a given study site using average solar conditions and typical amounts and
distributions of suspended dust in the atmosphere.
Our reply: We recognize the concerns of the reviewer regarding the assumptions and limited
spatial resolution of many of the used auxiliary datasets, such as WEH and environmental (MCD)
parameters. However, these datasets 1) represent some of the most relevant, potential drivers of
streak formation, such as wind action, and 2) are the state-of-the-art, or in other words, the best
data we currently have access to. We briefly express these deliberations in the manuscript, e.g.:
Note that the relatively low spatial resolution of most of the global thermophysical datasets might blur
certain relations, most prominently for the MOLA slope angle dataset, which largely underestimates
the actual slope angle.
However, we agree with the reviewer that there needs to be a specific, detailed discussion of any
potential negative impact on the scientific results of this work. We added a dedicated paragraph to
the “Geostatistical analysis & auxiliary dataset limitations” section:
Importantly, many of the used global auxiliary datasets feature spatial resolutions several factors
below the size of CTX-detected slope streaks and/or depend on various assumptions and models, such
as the MCD-derived outputs. For example, the global, km-scale, MCD-derived wind speed maps do not
fully capture the complex influence of small-scale topography on wind speed and direction. We
underline the importance of local, site-specific studies to verify the global-scale observations and
interpretations made by this work.
We note that the results related to WEH specifically are not vital to the scientific conclusions of this
work; they are merely complimentary and were integrated into the manuscript following
community feedback as provided for some of our preliminary slope streak mapping results.
Conclusion of review
Bickel & Valantinas have taken up an interesting topic and have written an easy to comprehend
article with really very appealing illustrations. In view of the far-reaching conclusions, they want to
draw from their analysis of CTX images, it would have been much better to produce an unedited CNN
based catalogue as a supplement to the paper with all the necessary information produced by the
CNN (exact coordinates, thumbnails, image ID, confidence, etc.) A second catalogue which is
the result of what they call the expert review could have then been released. Based on this information a
detailed and reproducible discussion could have been started in which they have a chance to win
support for the various claims they make in their work.
Unfortunately, the authors use many of the data sets which they need in their argumentation too
"literally". I would recommend that they include some colleagues in their work who have worked on
the analysis of nuclear spectroscopic methods.
In the present form the article does not provide the reproducible evidence for the conclusions they
draw. I suggest to the authors that they use part of their work to investigate their hypotheses on a
more local scale where they are able to check their findings in more detail (many of the papers in their
reference list have done this).

detections, their respective confidence scores, etc., as requested: https://doi.org/10.48620/75966
We are convinced that an expert-reviewed and science-ready catalog offers the greatest scientific
value and reproducibility. This curated dataset can be directly overlaid on the Dickson global CTX
23

underline that the scope and methodology of our study focuses primarily on geomorphological

streak-scale, they represent the state-of-the-art; in other words, these datasets are the best we
currently have available. In addition, all of the concerns put forward by the reviewer regarding the
methodology such as duplicate detections or image quality issues – if present at all – would not
systematically affect the results of this work.
Further, we would like to stress that the results of this work are fully reproducible – the used
object detector and data are openly available, and all plots in the manuscript can be reproduced
using the associated dataset and the various, publicly available auxiliary datasets.
This work represents a significant leap forward, lifting slope streak-related research from an
image-level (thousands of streak-bearing images) to an individual streak-level (hundreds of
thousands of individual slope streaks). We integrated substantial revisions of the text, figures, and
tables in both the main text, Online Methods section, as well as the supplementary information,
and – notably – slightly exceed the maximum permissible word count for the Online Methods
section. We hope that our revisions can address all of the reviewer’s concerns about our dataset
and the associated results and interpretations.
